Questions:
Q1: Does this apply to students whose DLl is not specifically mentioned on a study permit? For example, DLI Alberta?
A1: Yes, the regulation applies to all study permit holders regardless of whether their DLl is specifically mentioned on their study permit or not.
Q2: If a student is withdrawn from the program, and their study permit becomes invalid, can they/do they need to apply to restore their status as a student if they are accepted into another program at the same DLl shortly after the withdrawal?
A2: A study permit holder must meet their study permit conditions. In such cases where the student is withdrawn due to not meeting previous study permit conditions, the student is considered "no longer enrolled". If you do not abide to the conditions of your study permit you may need to change your status, or leave Canada. However, there are a few cases where a student may be able to take a leave of up to a maximum of 150 days from their program of studies and still be actively pursuing their studies.
For more information, please refer to the [RCC website.
Q3: Sometimes students could be withdrawn for non-payment, but after paying the fees in full, they could be reinstated. It could take about a week for us to re-instate the student. In this case, does their study permit become invalid the day they are withdrawn, or they can continue studying after being reinstated?
A3: See above.
Q4: What is IRCC's definition of enrolment for the purpose of this provision? Is it being active in the program or being enrolled in and taking classes? Students could be active in the program while on a scheduled break or an authorized leave, but they are not enrolled in classes during that time.
A4: A student is considered enrolled if they are actively attending classes or registered for courses at their DLl excluding regularly scheduled breaks, and authorized leave of up to 150 days. Students will need to ensure that they meet the conditions of their study permit Your conditions as a study permit holder in Canada-Canada.ca. Therefore, while students are not actively taking classes during regularly scheduled breaks or authorized leave of up to 150 days, they are still considered as being enrolled in their DLI.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

De : Envoyé : 28 janvier 2025 15:22 À : Objet : RE: Online courses and PGWP-REP-2024-1340- Due 3-Sep-24
Hello!
The recently announced IRCC regulations indicate that international students with valid study permits may need to apply for a new study permit when changing their designated learning institution (DLl) in most situations. However, there are scenarios (below) that do not clearly align with the examples provided on the IRCC guidelines page. [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/change-schools.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/change-schools.html)
1. Scenario 1: Prerequisite Courses at a Secondary Institution A student is currently enrolled in a degree program at a university (DLI) but requires prerequisite high school courses. These courses would be attended simultaneously at a secondary school while the student remains enrolled in their degree program at the university. Since the student is not changing their primary institution but is attending a single course at a secondary school, would they still be required to apply for a new study permit to take this course?
A: Secondary students whose permit only authorizes studies at the primary or secondary level must apply for a new study permit in order to pursue studies at the post-secondary level. This also applies to post-secondary study permit holders, whose permit names a DLl or limits their studies to the post-secondary level, who wish to attend a secondary school program/course, even though the student is not changing their primary institution. Therefore, individuals transitioning between post-secondary and secondary level need to get a new study permit by applying to extend their current one to attend a secondary school.
and Cizenship Caneda
2.Scenario 2: Cross-Institutional Enrollment for a Single Course Some students encounter situations where a required course is unavailable at their current university (DLl). In such cases, they obtain a letter of permission from their primary institution to take the course at another DLI (university) for one term, with the intention of transferring the credit back to their primary DLI (the one listed on their study permit). In this scenario, since the student is not permanently changing their DLl but is only attending a single course at another institution temporarily,would they need to apply for a new study permit?
A: Since November 08, 2024, post-secondary study permit holders must be enrolled at the designated learning institution (DLl) named on their permit. If a study permit holder wishes to concurrently attend more than one DLl, they must apply for a study permit for each DLl at which they intend to study.
As these scenarios are not explicitly addressed in the current guidelines, clarification on these matters would greatly help us provide accurate advice to international students.
Thank you for your guidance.
Regards,

Follow up question: Do I understand this correctly that if a student's study permit becomes invalid due to being withdrawn from their DLl, they lose their valid status in Canada? If yes, they are not authorized to change their status with Canada. If this is the case, do they need to:
In case they want to restore their status as a student, apply for a study permit restoration? In case they want to change their status to a visitor, apply for a restoration and a visitor's record?
Answer: A student is no longer registered or enrolled when the DLl has sent a letter informing the student that they've been dismissed, withdrawn or transferred to another institution. Their study permit becomes invalid as per R222(1)(a.1), even if the document is not expired. Therefore, they would need to change their status or leave Canada. Please note that applying for a restoration would only be possible if the document has expired. A foreign national has 90 days from the date of expiry date to submit a restoration application.
Q4: What is IRCC's definition of enrolment for the purpose of this provision? Is it being active in the program or being enrolled in and taking classes? Students could be active in the program while on a scheduled break or an authorized leave, but they are not enrolled in classes during that time. A4: A student is considered enrolled if they are actively attending classes or registered
for courses at their DLl excluding regularly scheduled breaks, and authorized leave of up
to 150 days. Students will need to ensure that they meet the conditions of their study
permit Your conditions as a study permit holder in Canada-Canada.ca. Therefore, while
students are not actively taking classes during regularly scheduled breaks or authorized
leave of up to 150 days, they are still considered as being enrolled in their DLI. Follow up questions:
If a student is registered in classes, but starts their program in let's say four months, are they considered enrolled at a DLI by IRCC for the purpose of this regulation for four months
until they start classes? Every term, we have several students who are withdrawn from a
program, but are planning to start a different program in one term.
If a student is withdrawn from a program, has a LOA for a different program that starts in 4 months, but is not registered in classes yet, are they considered enrolled at a DLl by IRCC
for the purpose of this regulation for four months until they start classes?
Answer: As indicated above, a student is no longer registered or enrolled when the DLl has sent a letter informing the student that they've been dismissed, withdrawn or transferred to another institution. Their study permit becomes invalid as per R222(1)(a.1), even if the document is not expired. Please note that an academic withdrawal is not considered an authorized leave in which the student is no longer considered an active student. Therefore, they would need to change their status or leave Canada.
In comparison, an academic suspension would be considered a leave. A student may take leave for a maximum 150 days due to academic suspension and would not be considered as no longer being registered or enrolled. The student would be allowed to return to their studies after the suspension. Please note that the enrollment status as " no longer registered/enrolled" and " academic suspension" are not the same. Please note that any leave over 150 days is not allowed, and the student would either need to change their status or leave Canada.
The IRCC website provides a glossary with definitions about the enrollment status of a student at a DLl such as academic suspension, no longer registered or enrolled, authorized leave etc.
Thank you kindly,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Question 1:
Maintained Status After IEC YP VIE Expiry If a foreign national is under maintained status following the expiry of their IEC Young Professionals (VIE) work permit, are they allowed to continue working for the same employer during the processing period if they are no longer being remunerated by Business France? Or does this change in employment conditions require them to cease working until their new work permit application is approved? Generally speaking, must their salary and benefits remain the exact same in order for them to continue working during the processing of their new work permit application?
Response 1:
When applying for a subsequent lEC participation, lEC participants do not meet the requirements for maintained status and are not authorized to work without a permit. Participants may only work while their work permit is valid, regardless if the conditions are the same or not.
Question 2:
Maintained Status After Application for a Different Temporary Resident Status If a foreign national submits an application to change their status (e.g., from worker to visitor) before their work permit
expires, thereby triggering maintained status, are they allowed to continue working under the same conditions of their expired work permit while the new application is being processed? Or must they cease working after their work permit expires and await the decision on their new temporary residence application?
Response 2:
Please note that IRCC cannot provide guidance regarding specific case inquiries or hypothetical scenarios.
An applicant benefits from maintained status if they submit an application to extend or change the conditions of their stay before the expiry date on their status document or, if no status document was issued, before the end of the 6-month period of authorized stay for foreign nationals who entered Canada as a visitor.
If an applicant who previously held a work or study permit applies for a visitor record before the expiry of their permit, they may benefit from maintained status during the processing period of the visitor record application, but they do not have the authorization to work or study after the expiry of their permit. See Temporary residents: Maintained status during processing (previously called implied status) - Canada.ca for more information.

To whom it may concern,
I understand that in most cases married couples and common-law partners are recommended to file a PR application as a family such that one of them will be the principal applicant while the other will be the dependent. However, if the common-law partners want to apply for PR on their own merits such that their chance of approval won't be affected by a change in their relationship in the future, is that possible? To provide more context, an example is a PR application under the public policy for Hong Kong residents, a common-law couple may want to file their own PR application independently without declaring their common-law partnership, which I know would put them at risk of misrepresentation. threads.answer:
Good afternoon,
As you've correctly noted, not declaring a common law relationship would be considered misrepresentation.
Applicants can have multiple applications for PR open at the same time. They can have an application in the SCLP class as well as an application in the HK Public Policy stream. When/if PRis received the other application would be cancelled and there would be no refund for the processing fees.

Question A) : If a Canadian corporation and the attendant applicants applying for permanent residence who are being supported by a government-approved Incubator that is not listed as a priority designated organization referenced above, from the current inventory of pending applications for permanent residence under the start up business class, that were submitted prior to April 30, 2024, receives a term sheet from the incubator for a $75,000 investment commitment, would such a commitment qualify as "committed capital" as defined in the relevant operational bulletin? Further, would this result in the applicants associated with the commitment certificate, being supported by the Incubator, receiving prioritization by ClO?
Answer : Yes, this application would be considered prioritized under the current Start-Up Visa prioritization:
Although the incubator is not part of Canada's Tech Network (CTN), the $75,000 investment commitment meets the capital threshold required for prioritization. Specifically: Angel investor groups and venture capital funds need only show they have committed the required amount of capital to the applicant's business; there is no additional prioritization screening, so almost all applicants they sponsor are automatically prioritized.
For business incubators, prioritization depends on whether the incubator is part of the CTN:
oIf the incubator is in the CTN, applicants are automatically prioritized. 0If the incubator is not in the CTN, applicants can still be prioritized if they have secured at least $75,000 in committed capital.
Since this scenario meets the second condition, it qualifies for prioritization even if the application was submitted before April 30, 2024.
Question B) : If a Canadian corporation and the attendant applicants applying for permanent residence who are being supported by a government-approved Incubator that is not listed as a priority designated organization referenced above, from the current inventory of pending applications for permanent residence under the start up business class, that were submitted prior to April 30, 2024, receives a term sheet for a $75,000 investment commitment from an approved Angel Investor group identified in the above list, would such a commitment qualify as "committed capital" as defined in the relevant operational bulletin? Further, would this result in the
applicants associated with the commitment certificate, being supported by an Incubator, receiving prioritization by the CIO under the Start-Up Visa Program?
Answer : Yes, this application would be prioritized under the current Ministerial Instructions for the Start-Up Business Class. Specifically:
- A $75,000 investment commitment from a designated Angel Investor group qualifies as “committed capital” according to the Ministerial Instructions. The application does not need support from a CTN-member incubator to be prioritized since the prioritization is based on the angel investor's commitment.
These instructions apply to all applications, including those submitted before April 30, 2024, as long as the commitment meets the specified criteria.
The Ministerial Instructions state that all Start-Up Business Class applications, including those submitted before the effective date, will be prioritized if supported by a commitment that meets certain conditions—one being a minimum investment of $75,000 from an authorized angel investor group. Therefore, your application meets the prioritization criteria, and the CiO will prioritize it accordingly.
Please be advised that the assessment of each application is done on a case-by-case basis, taking into account the specific circumstances and supporting documentation provided. It is the applicant's responsibility to ensure that sufficient documentation is submitted to demonstrate compliance with the program's requirements.

Des étudiants qui étaient au secondaire l’an dernier et qui entrent au cégep à l’automne 2025, nous confirment que des agents d’IRCC leur ont dit qu’ils pouvaient commencer leurs études au cégep sans avoir reçu leur permis d’études, dans certaines circonstances, par exemple si l’étudiant possède une fiche visiteur. En réponse à vos questions numérotées 1 et 2, veuillez noter que les étudiants qui passent du niveau secondaire au niveau postsecondaire doivent obtenir un permis d'études pour les études postsecondaires en présentant une demande pour faire prolonger leur séjour au Canada à titre d'étudiant (prolongation du permis d'études). Une fois leur demande présentée, ils peuvent poursuivre leurs études au niveau postsecondaire en attendant la décision concernant leur nouvelle demande de permis d'études. Si leur demande de permis d'études est refusée, ils doivent cesser immédiatement leurs études. Si toutefois, leur permis d'études mentionne un établissement d'enseignement désigné (EED) spécifique, ils doivent attendre que leur demande de permis d'études soit approuvée avant de commencer leurs études.
En réponse votre question numérotée 3, les étudiants qui étaient admissibles à étudier au niveau secondaire avec une fiche visiteur doivent également demander un permis d'études pour pouvoir étudier au niveau postsecondaire en soumettant une demande pour faire prolonger leur séjour au Canada à titre d'étudiant. Veuillez noter qu'ils ne peuvent pas commencer leurs études au niveau postsecondaire tant que leur permis d'études n'a pas été approuvé.
Nous espérons que ces informations vous seront utiles.
Cordialement,
La boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration

Les directives indiquent : Il est possible que l’étudiant souhaite ou doive interrompre temporairement ses études pendant son séjour au Canada. Lorsqu’il s’agit d’évaluer si l’étudiant poursuit activement ses études, tout congé d’un programme d’études au Canada ne doit pas dépasser 150 jours à compter de la date de début du congé, et le congé doit avoir été autorisé par l’EED.
On considère qu'un étudiant en congé qui commence ou reprend ses études dans les 150 jours qui suivent la date de début du congé (c'est-à-dire la date à laquelle l’établissement lui a accordé un congé) poursuit activement ses études pendant son congé. Si l’étudiant ne reprend pas ses études dans les 150 jours, il doit suivre un des 2 scénarios suivants :
changer son statut (c'est-à-dire changer pour un statut de visiteur ou un statut de travailleur); quitter le Canada.
S’il ne change pas son statut ou ne quitte pas le Canada, il est réputé non conforme aux conditions liées à son permis d’études.
Les étudiants qui cessent leurs études et ne sont pas autorisés par leur établissement d'enseignement désigné à prendre congé peuvent être considérés comme ne respectant pas les conditions de leur permis d'études. Ce manquement peut avoir une incidence négative sur leur future demande. Par exemple, un permis de travail subséquent pourrait ne pas être délivré avant six mois, après la cessation des études non autorisées ou le non- respect d'une condition, conformément à l'alinéa 221a) et au sous-alinéa R200(3)(e)(i).

As indicated on our website, the amount of work experience that was required is based on when IRCC assesses the application, which means the most recent change in the work experience requirement to 6 months applies to all applications pending a final decision, regardless of when the application was submitted.
For example:
- If an applicant submits their proof of work experience after June 16, 2024, they would only be required to submit proof of at least 6 months of experience, regardless of when they applied or when the Stage 1 decision (pre- assessment of permanent residence eligibility and issuance of the occupation-restricted open work permit) had been made.
- If an application was refused on June 1, 2024 because the applicant didn't have sufficient work experience (i.e., 12 months), the application would not be re-opened on June 17th and re-assessed for 6 months of work experience, since at the time a decision was made on the application, the requirement was 12 months.
- If an applicant submitted their proof of work experience when the required experience was 12 months, but IRCC assessed that proof after June 16, 2024, they would be assessed for 6 months. For applications submitted under the Gaining experience category, the work experience can be either from within Canada or overseas. Any work experience gained in Canada must be authorized. The work can be authorized under any combination of authorized work permits or authorizations, acquired while the applicant had temporary resident status, as long as the applicant was not engaged in full-time study. This means that the work experience can be from a work permit issued under the International Mobility Program or the Temporary Foreign Worker Program, including a post- graduate work permit (PGWP), Live-in Caregiver program (LCP) work permit, work permits issued under the International Experience Canada (IEC) program (e.g., working holiday work permit), etc. For the Gaining experience category applications, while experience gained on any work authorizations outside of the occupation-restricted open work permit (OROWP) can count, the deadline for submitting proof of work experience is still 36 months following OROWP issuance.
As applicants are now able to use Canadian or foreign work experience, or a combination of both, to satisfy the work experience requirement, they may have 6 months of work experience that they obtained before they were even issued an OROWP that is now eligible. However, eligible work experience must have been accumulated no more than 36 months before the initial application was submitted. For example, if an applicant submitted their application for permanent residence on June 1, 2021, they can only use eligible work experience obtained after June 1, 2018 (and up to 36 months after issuance of the OROWP). In all cases, it is important that the applicant carefully reviews all documentation to ensure they meet the work experience requirement before sending their proof, as a decision will be made based on the information that is provided.
For applications submitted under the direct to permanent residence category (Category B), the work experience can only be Canadian, and obtained within the 36 months before the application was submitted.
For more information, refer to our website:

For International Experience Canada (lEC), if a temporary resident applies for a work permit renewal (extension) in a category outside of the lEC program while their lEC work permit is still valid, they receive the authorization to work without a permit under paragraph R186(u), and the conditions of their lEC work permit continue until a decision is made. This period of time when they are authorized to work without a permit is not considered an extension of their IEC participation.
If the temporary foreign worker is renewing with the same employer but different conditions, paragraph R186(u) applies and they are authorized to work; however, while waiting for a decision, the worker must continue to comply with the original conditions.
Pursuant to subsection R209.2(2), the period of employment for the employer conditions listed in section 209.2 includes any period during which the temporary resident was authorized to work under paragraph R186(u) after the expiry of their work permit. Therefore, the employer continues to be subject to the conditions and may be subject to inspection until a decision is made on the subsection R201(1) application. This does not necessarily mean the salary must be exactly the same, rather, as per R209.2(1)(jii), the employer must provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer.

Dear Officer,
I am writing as a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCiC) to request confirmation regarding
the eligibility requirements for spousal open work permits issued under subparagraph Immigration and
Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) R205(c)(ii), administrative code C41, following the changes
effective January 2025.
As per the current Program Delivery Instructions and Operational Bulletin (OB) updates, it is my understanding that, at the time of decision on the spousal work permit application, the principal foreign national must meet the following conditions:
1. Authorization to Work in Canada 0Must hold a valid work permit, provisional approval (letter of introduction), or authorization
to work under IRPR section R186 (excluding R186(f), R186(v), or R186(w)); 0 The work permit must not have been issued under exemptions such as: R204(a) – FTA spousal open work permits R205(a) – RNIP spouses (C17), HCCPP/HSWP spouses and dependents (C91) R205(c)(i.1 or i.2) – Co-op work permits for students (C32, C33) R205(c)(ii) – other family member OWP categories (C42, C46–C49) R206 – Refugee claimants (S61, S62)
2. Duration of Authorization
The principal foreign national must be authorized (or provisionally approved) to work in Canada for at least 16 months from the date of receipt of the spousal open work permit application (IRPR R200(1)(c)(ii)).
3. Employment Requirements The principal must be employed, or have arranged employment, in:
A TEER 0 (management) or TEER 1 (professional) occupation, OR
A TEER 2 or TEER 3 occupation as specifically listed in Annex A of the updated instructions.
4. Other Conditions The principal must be physically residing in Canada or have the intention to do so while
employed.
The relationship between the applicant and the principal must be a genuine spousal or
common-law partnership (IRPR R4.1). OIf the applicant is applying from within Canada, they must hold valid temporary resident status, including maintained status (R183(5)), or be eligible for restoration (R182), and be permitted to apply for a work permit in Canada (R199).

TEER 2/3 roles, are no longer eligible.

Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the RCC Web form.

Please note that this service provides guidance and not case-specific advice. Therefore, our response reflects general information on work permits. While we cannot provide case-specific recommendations or immigration advice on work permit options for hypothetical scenarios, please refer to the Temporary Workers General Eligibility Requirements in order to determine the work permit options available under the Temporary Foreign Worker Program and the International Mobility Program.
Response to question 1:
Applicants who meet the requirements under paragraph R186(u) may receive an acknowledgment of receipt letter (AoR) from IRCC indicating the continued authorization to work. If the applicant submitted the subsequent application after the expiry of their initial work permit, the AoR will not be sent automatically, and the applicants cannot ask for one through the IRCC web form.
Response to question 2:
A work permit applicant may continue working under the same conditions as their previous work permit until a decision is made on their extension application if they have applied to extend their stay in Canada as a worker [R186(u)] before their initial work permit expires. If they had an OWP when they applied to extend their authorization to work, they may continue to work with any employer and in any location as per the conditions in the initial OWP until a decision is made on the extension application.
If a second or a subsequent WP application is received during processing of the first application but before the original status and work authorization expired, the applicant continues to maintain their status and is authorized to work without a permit under R186(u) until a decision is made, provided they remain in Canada and continue to meet the requirements of R186(u).

Dear IRCC,

2. If the clients decide to change their current inland spousal sponsorship to an outland application due to temporary travel, would this require submitting a new application and losing the progress already made?
3. For an outland spousal sponsorship, if the applicant leaves Canada temporarily and plans to return within a few months with the Canadian sponsor and their newborn, would there be any implications for re-entry or the continuation of the process?
We appreciate your guidance so we can advise our clients on the most appropriate course of action.

October 9, 2025 11:51 AM
FW: (CPD-2025-0539) FW: Request for Guidance – Proof of Citizenship vs. Sponsorship
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the RCC Web form.
Please see our response to your question.
1. Based on our understanding, the child may be eligible for Canadian citizenship by descent. My clients wish to confirm whether applying for a Proof of Citizenship and subsequently a Canadian passport would make it unnecessary to include the child in the sponsorship application.
A child born overseas to a Canadian citizen parent may be eligible for citizenship by descent, provided certain conditions are met. See Check if you may be a citizen and Am I a Canadian? for more information.
Generally, if the Canadian citizen parent was either born in Canada or became a naturalized Canadian citizen before the child was born, the child is likely eligible for Canadian citizenship by descent. Based on the information provided, this appears to be the likely case however we cannot confirm citizenship status for an unborn child, especially as the rules for citizenship by descent are changing.
The child's parents are encouraged to apply for proof of Canadian citizenship once the child is born, as this is the formal way to find out if a person is a citizen. Should the parents choose to proceed via the citizenship route, there would be no need to include the child in the immigration sponsorship application; however, they must provide proof of citizenship (a citizenship certificate) when applying for the child's passport. It is important to note that the parents should apply for the child's Canadian citizenship documentation before attempting to travel to Canada, as it serves as the official proof that they are a Canadian citizen. Furthermore, Canadian citizens can no longer travel to Canada by air with a non-Canadian passport. See Dual Canadian citizens need a valid Canadian passport for more information.
If it is determined that the child does not have a claim to citizenship by descent, the parents may still choose to sponsor their child as a permanent resident under the IRPA and apply for Canadian citizenship at a later date.
1. If the child is born abroad and obtains Canadian citizenship by descent, would there be any requirement to include her in the ongoing sponsorship process?
As noted above, there would be no requirement to include the child in the spousal sponsorship application as a dependent, if the parents are choosing to submit a citizenship application.
中 et Cioyenneté Canada
2. If the clients decide to change their current inland spousal sponsorship to an outland application due to temporary travel, would this require submitting a new application and losing the progress already made?
Applicants applying under the overseas family class stream or Spouse or Common-Law Partner in Canada class (SCLPC) stream must meet the requirements of the stream under which they've applied throughout the application process. As both streams have different requirements, it would not be possible to convert the application from the overseas to the in-Canada stream or vice versa. Generally, a sponsor should apply under the Family Class if the person they want to sponsor currently lives with them in Canada, but does not plan to stay in Canada while the application is being processed. Should the sponsor and the principal applicant decide to change their Spouse or Common-Law Partner in Canada (SCLPC) application to a Family Class application, the SCLPC application would have to be withdrawn and a new application submitted.
Applicants applying under the spouse or common-law partner in Canada class must cohabit with their sponsor in Canada. As noted in the Complete Guide, leaving Canada can automatically cancel temporary resident status as a visitor, student or worker. If the applicant leaves Canada before becoming a permanent resident, they may not be allowed to come back. This is especially true if they need a Temporary Resident Visa or an eTA to enter Canada. The border services officer at the port of entry will determine whether a foreign national is authorized to enter Canada. If your spouse or partner can't return to Canada, they will not longer meet the requirements of the in Canada class and they will need to submit a new overseas sponsorship application.
3. For an outland spousal sponsorship, if the applicant leaves Canada temporarily and plans to return within a few months with the Canadian sponsor and their newborn, would there be any implications for re-entry or the continuation of the process
As there is no requirement under the overseas family class for an applicant to be in or remain in Canada, leaving Canada during the processing of the spousal sponsorship application would not have an impact on their eligibility under the family class. That said, if an applicant applying under the overseas Family Class is in Canada, they must comply with the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and Regulations. This includes maintaining their valid temporary resident status while they are in Canada. Failure to do so could result in them being found inadmissible and their application for permanent residence being refused.
There is no guarantee that a foreign national will be allowed to re-enter Canada. The onus is on the applicant to ensure they have the proper documentation required to enter Canada and are not inadmissible. The border services officer at the port of entry will determine whether a foreign national is authorized to enter Canada.
We hope you find this information useful.
Thank you kindly,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.question:

Bonjour,
Nous aimerions savoir si des étudiants qui ont diplômé d’un premier programme d’études peuvent en commencer un 2º en bénéficiant de l’article R189 (étudier sans permis d’études), suite à une demande de prorogation de permis d’études présentée alors que le permis antérieur est devenu invalide par l’application de l’article R222(1)a)?
Voici un exemple de scénario :
Étudiant termine un premier programme avec un permis d’études encore valide pour 6-12 mois après l’obtention du diplôme.
Étudiants présentent la demande (et obtient) le permis de travail postdiplome. Permis d’études devient invalide 90 jours après avoir terminé les études [R222(1)a)]. Étudiant veut retourner aux études (dans le même EED). Étudiant présente une demande de permis d’études, entre le moment où le permis d’études précédent devient invalide et l’expiration de ce dernier. Est-ce que cette demande est considérée comme un renouvellement de son permis d’études présenté avant son expiration [R217]? Ou, est-ce que cette demande est considérée comme une nouvelle demande [R215] malgré le fait que la personne détient un permis d’études non-expiré? ●Si cette demande est considérée comme un renouvellement [R217], peut-il bénéficier du droit d’étudier sans permis d’études en vertu du R189?
Si oui, durant quelle période?
Dès le dépôt de la demande du 2° permis d’études 0Uniquement durant la période entre l’expiration du 1er permis d’études et la réception du 2º permis d’études.
Nous nous posons la question, car l’article R217(1) fait référence à une demande présentée avant l’expiration du permis d’études, mais ne mentionne rien en regard à la validité du dit permis
Un permis peut-il être invalide, mais non expiré, et toujours donner des autorisations en vertu de la LiPR?
Est-ce que votre réponse est différente si l’invalidité du permis découle de l’application de R222(1)a.1) et non du R222(1)a)?
Pouvez-vous confirmer que les conditions auxquelles font référence l’article R189 et l’article R217(1)b) sont celles des articles R183(1), R185 et R220.1 (1)?
Est-ce qu’une personne qui a été diplômée et qu1 détient un permis d’études non-expiré, mais invalide suite à l’application de l’article R222(1)a) est dispensée des conditions de l’article R220.1(1) ?
Merci de votre support
Ghazal, Reda (IRCC/IRCC)
threads.answer:
Bonjour,
Merci d’avoir contacté la boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration.
Veuillez noter que cette boîte aux lettres est destinée à fournir des conseils généraux et ne fournit pas de réponses à des demandes spécifiques à un cas, mais a fourni les informations suivantes comme conseil. Si vous avez des questions spécifiques à un dossier, nous vous encourageons à soumettre le formulaire Formulaire Web d'IRCC-Canada.ca
Veuillez consulter notre réponse à votre question.
Lorsqu'un étudiant diplômé présente une demande de permis d'études après que son permis est devenu invalide en vertu de l’article R222(1)(a), mais avant la date d’expiration officielle du permis, cette demande n’est pas considérée comme une prorogation selon l’article R217, car le permis est invalide, même s’il n’est pas encore expiré. Elle est donc traitée comme une nouvelle demande en vertu de l’article R215. Par conséquent, l’article R189, qui permet à un étudiant de poursuivre ses études sans permis pendant le traitement d’une demande de prorogation valide, ne s’applique pas. L’étudiant ne peut donc pas reprendre ses études tant que le nouveau permis n’a pas été délivré.
Un permis d’études peut être non expiré mais tout de même invalide, notamment en vertu des articles R222(1)(a) ou R222(1)(a.1). Dans ces situations, le permis ne confère plus de statut ni d’autorisation en vertu de la Loi sur l’immigration et la protection des réfugiés.
Enfin, une personne détenant un permis d’études non expiré mais invalide selon R222(1)a) n’est pas exemptée des conditions prévues à l’article R220.1(1) et doit attendre l’approbation d’un nouveau permis avant de pouvoir reprendre ses études.
Cordialement,
La boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration

I am and I would like to kindly request clarification regarding the "lock-in date” for the age of dependent children in permanent residence applications submitted through the PR Portal.
Specifically, in programs such as the Caregiver pilot, where applicants submitted their applications on March 31, 2025, if the applicant's child was under 22 years of age on the date of submission (via PR Portal), but turned 22 on May 30, 2025 before the Acknowledgement of Receipt (AOR) was issued, would the child still be considered a dependent and included in the application? As you know, it often takes several months for applicants to receive an AOR in these types of programs.
In other words, for applications submitted online via the PR Portal (such as Caregiver, Start-Up Visa, Spousal Sponsorship, or Parents Sponsorship), is the dependent child's age locked-in at the date of submission of the complete application through the PR Portal, or at the date when the AOR and file number are issued?

Ghazal, Reda (IRCC/IRCC)
threads.answer:
October 9, 2025 11:50 AM
FW: Question Regarding Age Lock-In Date for Dependent Children in PR Portal
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the RCC Web form.
Please see our response to your question.
Age lock-in dates vary by immigration program or category. Whether your child is eligible as a dependant depends on how old they are on that date. For most programs, your child's age lock-in date is the date we get your complete application for permanent residence. Some programs have several steps, so your child's age is locked in before you submit your complete application for permanent residence.
For example, for Home Care Worker Immigration pilot applications, the age of a dependent child is locked in on the date of receipt of the principal applicant's complete permanent residence application. A complete permanent residence application contains all of the items in the document checklist for the specific category, which includes proof of payment of the correct processing fees. The date that IRCC reviews the application for completeness and issues the acknowledgement of receipt (AOR) does not determine the lock-in date.

To qualify for the Home Care Worker Immigration pilots, applicants must have enough relevant work experience OR training. Applicants must have either 6 months of continuous, full-time and relevant work experience in the past 3 years OR completed a relevant training credential in the past 2 years before they apply. Please see here for more information regarding qualifying work experience and training. As per paragraph R185(b), an officer may impose specific conditions on a temporary resident, including the work they are both permitted to engage in or prohibited from engaging in while in Canada. If an applicant's work permit has remarks that they are not authorized to work in child care or health services field occupations, any work that they undertake as a home child care provider or home support worker would be considered unauthorized. These conditions would typically be imposed on individuals who have not undergone a medical examination, to ensure they do not take a job that requires close contact with people, such as care for children, the elderly and the disabled, in order to protect public health.
2. Is experience working in a senior care home eligible for the Caregiver Pilot Program that will reopen in 2026? Under the Home Care Worker Immigration Pilot Home Support stream, applicants must have recent and relevant work experience or training. The work experience for the Home Care Worker Immigration Pilots must:
be in 1 or both of the National Occupational Classifications (NOCs) of the pilot they apply for HCWIP: Home Support Home support workers, caregivers and related occupations (NOC 44101) Nurse aides, orderlies and patient service associates (NOC 33102) Work experience in NOC 33102 gained in an institutional setting (for example, long-term care) may be eligible. •Must be in the NOCs of 1 pilot—either child care or home support.
The work experience must match the NoC job description and include most of the main duties listed under the NOC. Please see here for more information regarding work experience.
Applicants must also have a genuine and valid job offer for full-time employment in the home support worker occupation in Canada (NOC 44101) to be eligible. The job offer must demonstrate the applicant will be providing personal care services, not health or nursing services, in a residential setting.
NoC 44101: Home support workers, caregivers and related occupations, provide personal care and companionship for seniors, persons with disabilities and convalescent clients. They provide care in the client's residence, where they may also reside. They are employed by home care and support agencies, private households, or they may be self-employed.
Job offer eligibility depends on the specific nature of the caregiving role. If the caregiving work involves providing personal care services in a residential setting the job offer may qualify. Officers will use all available information to determine whether the applicant will be providing services that align with the NOC and whether the work setting is considered the care recipient's private residence. If the work will extend beyond personal care services and is offered in an institution, it may be ineligible.
Please see here for more information regarding job offers, and here for more information regarding eligible employers.

Le fait de déposer une demande de résidence permanente (RP) pour considérations humanitaires n'empêche pas

Bonjour,
Au regard des modifications faites par IRCC en novembre dernier, j’aimerais avoir des précisions sur le cas suivant :
Des étudiants ont dû interrompre leur scolarité temporairement pour des raisons financières, ils ne sont pas admissibles à un congé autorisé par l’EED. Cependant, dans la mesure où ils respectent les conditions pendant leur interruption (maintien d’une assurance maladie et médicaments privée, ne travaillent pas), que la date d’expiration sur le permis d’études est en 2026 ou 2027 et que leur situation financière s’est régularisée, est-il possible pour eux de reprendre les études à la session suivante, avec le même permis d’études? Ainsi, dans le contexte d’un congé d’études non autorisé, est-ce que le permis d’études est encore valide pour reprendre malgré que la date d’expiration indique que oui?
Si le permis devient invalide, qu’elle est la procédure que les étudiants devraient faire pour régulariser leur
statut d’étudiant et être autorisés à reprendre les études? Merci,
Ghazal, Reda (IRCC/IRCC)
threads.answer:
3-Nov-25
Bonjour,
Merci d’avoir contacté la boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration.
Veuillez noter que cette boîte aux lettres est destinée à fournir des conseils généraux et ne fournit pas de réponses à des demandes spécifiques à un cas, mais a fourni les informations suivantes comme conseil. Si vous avez des questions spécifiques à un dossier, nous vous encourageons à soumettre le formulaire Formulaire Web d'IRCC-Canada.ca
Veuillez consulter notre réponse à votre question.
Conformément au paragraphe 220.1(1) du Règlement sur l'immigration et la protection des réfugiés (RIPR), le titulaire d’un permis d’études au Canada est assujetti aux deux conditions suivantes :
a. Il est inscrit à l’établissement d'enseignement désigné (EED) figurant sur son permis d’études et y demeure inscrit jusqu'à ce qu’il termine ses études;
b. Il suit activement son cours ou son programme d’études.
Il est possible que l’étudiant souhaite ou doive interrompre temporairement ses études pendant son séjour au Canada. Lorsqu'il s’agit d’évaluer si l’étudiant poursuit activement ses études, tout congé d’un programme d’études au Canada ne doit pas dépasser 150 jours à compter de la date de début du congé, et le congé doit avoir été autorisé par l’EED. Il doit quitter le Canada s’il ne respecte pas ces conditions et qu’il ne détient pas d’autre autorisation valide, tel qu’un permis de séjour temporaire, une fiche de visiteur, un permis de travail, ou ne dépose pas de demande pour changer de statut (c'est-à-dire changer pour un statut de visiteur ou un statut de travailleur).
Conformément à l’article R222(1)(a.1), un permis d'études devient invalide lorsque le titulaire du permis n'est plus inscrit à l’établissement d’enseignement désigné qui est nommé dans son permis, à moins qu'il n'ait terminé ses études. Si le permis d'études d'un étudiant devient invalide en vertu du paragraphe R222(1) et qu'il ne détient pas d'autre autorisation valide, telle qu'un permis de séjour temporaire, une fiche de visiteur, un permis de travail ou un nouveau permis d'études, il doit quitter le Canada. S'il souhaite revenir, il doit présenter une nouvelle demande depuis l'étranger.
Nous espérons que ces informations vous seront utiles.
Cordialement,
La boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration

Thank you for your enquiry regarding automatic notifications from the Citizenship Application Status Tracker.
The Citizenship Application Status Tracker is built using a one-to-one access model, meaning that access is granted based on the email address associated to the application and the client's Unique Client Identifier (UCl).
When a client or representative creates an account, by entering the UCl and Application number, the Tracker will send a confirmation code by email to the email address associated to the application. If a representative receives the code, it is because someone started the account creation process. If it is a client (assuming they would have the application number which would have been sent to the representative), the representative will receive the confirmation code. A confirmation code is also sent to the email address on file when a client/representative attempts to recover a lost password.
For security reasons, the account registration process cannot be completed without the confirmation code. Also for security reasons, IRCC cannot provide personal information, such as a UCl or application number, with the confirmation code. Only the date and time that the code request was triggered is included for reference as the confirmation code is valid for 24 hours.
If a client using a representative knows their application number, they could initiate the account creation process, which would send the confirmation code to their representative's email address. Information is available, on the Citizenship Application Status Tracker and IRCC help pages, to explain that the confirmation code email will be send to the representative's email address for clients who are using a representative. If a client contacts IRCC because they have not received the confirmation code email, our agents will remind them that the email address associated to their application is that of their representative and to contact their representative to get case status updates.
This is likely the reason why a representative could be receiving the confirmation email without having initiated the account creation process. If this is the case, representatives can ignore the email with the confirmation code.

On December 19, 2023, the Ontario Superior Court of Justice declared that key provisions setting out the first-generation limit for those born abroad are unconstitutional. The Court suspended this declaration until November 20, 2025. To address the Court's decision while upholding the value of Canadian citizenship Bill C-3, An Act to amend the Citizenship Act (2025), was introduced in the House of Commons in order to make changes to the first-generation limit.
Until the period of invalidity to the Court's decision expires and changes to the rules on the first-generation limit to citizenship by descent come into force, the interim measure will remain in place for individuals who are impacted by the first-generation limit. To be considered under the interim measure applicants must complete an application for Citizenship certificate (i.e. proof of citizenship) or Adoption including necessary documentation outlined in the document checklist for the respective applications. Failure to provide a complete application including the necessary documentation may result in the rejection of the application.
Once the changes to the first-generation limit to citizenship by descent are in effect, applications impacted by the first-generation limit for proof or adoption will be processed in accordance with the rules in place at the time of processing and will no longer pass through the interim measure unless it is still applicable at that time. Applicants may choose to wait until the changes are in place to submit their applications – November 20, 2025 must not be viewed as a deadline for application submission rather it is an indication as to how the department handles the processing of the application.

1. If an applicant has valid biometrics on file from a previous application, can these still be used for a new Super Visa application submitted with a newly issued passport? Response: Yes, biometrics from a previous application can be re-used in support of a subsequent application assuming the biometrics are still valid. Please refer to the information below. Something to keep in mind is the validity of the Visa cannot be issued longer than the expiry of the Passport, or of the biometrics validity – whichever comes first.
Permanent residence applicants
Temporary resident to permanent resident: Valid biometrics provided to support a temporary residence application cannot be reused to support a permanent residence application.
Permanent resident to permanent resident: Biometrics provided to support a permanent residence application cannot be reused to support a subsequent or new permanent residence application. Applicants applying for permanent residence are required to enrol their biometrics to support every permanent residence application.
Permanent residence applicant to temporary residence applicant
Permanent resident to temporary resident: The biometrics can be reused to support a temporary residence application in cases where a foreign national has already provided the biometrics to support a permanent residence application, asylum claim, or overseas refugee resettlement application and is waiting for a decision on that application or claim.

If you want the Visa to be valid for a longer period, you can voluntarily provide new biometrics when applying, even if the previous ones haven't expired. In most cases, you'll need a new visa if you want to leave and come back to Canada You can ask to return to Canada on your original single-entry visitor visa only if: you'll only visit the U.S. or St. Pierre and Miquelon; and you'll return to Canada before the end of your approved stay in Canada.

Before travelling back to Canada

It is important to note that a temporary resident visa does not guarantee entry/re-entry, nor does it grant status in Canada. Please see our response to your question.
1. Is a Provincial/ Territorial Attestation Letter (PAL / TAL) Required for a student who has lost student status and is applying for restoration? A PAL or TAL is required for most initial study permit applications (i.e., to get a study permit when you apply to study in Canada). On the page for restoring status as a student (via “Extend your study permit or restore your status”): You may apply to restore your status (as a student) if your study permit expired and you meet the conditions. Under the new rules (2025) they a PAL is required for restoration of status as a student.
2. What are the options if a student loses status and the DLl cannot issue a PAL? If a student has lost status (i.e., their study permit expired before they applied for extension, or they did not maintain conditions) and the DLl or province cannot provide a PAL, the situation becomes more complex. Apply for restoration within 90 days of losing status: You must apply within 90 days of losing your status and you must have otherwise complied with your permit conditions. If you cannot obtain the PAL:
0Some DLls advise that if a PAL cannot be obtained (because of limited provincial allocation, etc.), the student may not be eligible for restoration and may have to consider applying for a new permit from outside Canada. If you lose status and you are outside the 90-day window, you must leave Canada and reapply for a new permit from abroad. 0If you cannot restore status as a student, you might apply to change your status (for example to visitor) while in Canada, although whether that is viable depends on your particular condition (and this would not allow you to study). If you are eligible you may switch status, but for students the usual route is restoration as student.
We hope that this information is helpful to you.

If a temporary resident is eligible to register with Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) for a business number and can meet other requirements for employers as per the offer of employment form, their status as a temporary resident (authorized to study or work) would not be a barrier to making the initial job offer.

Applicants for the Home Care Worker Immigration pilots must meet all requirements for the stream they apply to which includes needing a genuine job offer as a home child care provider or home support worker.
While there is no requirement for applicants to be currently working in the caregiving field, applicants must be likely to accept the job offer and be able to perform the job duties. We'll review things like their past training and experience to determine this.
For applicants under the Workers in Canada stream (stream A), the principal applicant must be residing in Canada when they apply. However, they could be physically outside of Canada when they apply (for example, on vacation), but still need to prove that they normally reside in Canada. Proof of residence in Canada could include:
a copy of a lease or rental agreement a letter from a landlord or property owner attesting to residence and specifying dates a copy of driver's license a copy of a bank statement or credit card statement with the applicant's address utility bills or any other bills that contain the applicant's residential address employment records or pay stubs Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) Notice of Assessment membership in professional, social or recreational organizations
Please note that once the application is submitted, the applicant does not need to continue to reside in Canada, while the application is being processed.

threads.question:
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
Hello Immigration Representatives,
My name is and I am a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant I'm reaching out to clarify whether a student can use their study permit work conditions (R. 186(f) and (v)) for work that is required to complete their program of study (i.e. co-op approved placements), or must the student apply for a co-op work permit to be authorized to work for these placements.
For example: a student will be completing their co-op placement off campus, the co-op placement requires a maximum of 15 hours per week – are they authorized to use their study permit conditions to work without applying for the co-op work permit.
Thank you for your clarification.
Best Regards,
Ghazal, Reda (IRCC/IRCC)
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the RCC Web form.
Please see our response to your question.
As listed in the eligibility under Work as a co-op student or intern-Canada.ca, students who require work to complete their program generally require a co-op WP. Work that is unrelated to the program may be eligible under Work off campus as an international student-Canada.ca and as you noted under Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations.
Students who are already in Canada and have applied for a co-op work permit may begin their co-op placement using their on-campus and off-campus work authorization, provided they meet all the eligibility requirements.
There is no limit on work hours for on-campus work. A student may accept employment on the campus of the university or college at which they are a full-time student under paragraph 186(f) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR).
For off-campus work authorization, as per paragraph R186(v), students can work a total of 24 hours per week during an academic term or semester while they are waiting for their co-op work permit; however, the 24 hours must include both the hours worked at their co-op job and those worked at their regular paid job (if they have one). They can work full-time during the regularly scheduled breaks.
We hope this information is of assistance.
Thank you kindly,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Foreign nationals may enter Canada or remain in Canada without a study permit to attend a course or program of study of 6 months' duration or less [R188(1)(c)]. This exemption helps to facilitate access to short-term courses, regardless of their subject matter. The course or program of study may be part-time or full-time and should be completed within the period authorized upon entry (max 6 months). Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the RCC Web form.
Please see our response to your question.
According to recent ministerial instructions, IRCC categorizes levels of study into three groups:
1. Primary and secondary education
2. Post-secondary education (including vocational and technical training, certificates, diplomas, advanced diplomas, and undergraduate programs)
3. Graduate education or above
Certificates, diplomas, and advanced diplomas (e.g., bachelor's degrees) all fall under post-secondary education. Students changing programs within the same level at the same Designated Learning Institution (DLl) do not need a new Provincial Attestation Letter (PAL) or territorial attestation letter (TAL). They can continue their studies at their DLI with their current study permit, provided they meet the permit conditions. However, if they need to extend their study permit, they must submit a new PAL/TAL.
A PAL/TAL is required if a student moves to a different level of study, such as from post-secondary to graduate education. If the Master program is considered as a graduate program at your DLl then students transitioning from a post secondary education level to a graduate level of education, must apply for a new study permit.
Students who remain within the same level of study while changing programs at the same designated learning institution (DLI) do not require a new PAL/TAL when applying for a study permit extension. For example, if the student wishes to change from one post-secondary program to another post-secondary program at the same DLl. However, a new PAL/TAL would be required if the student moves to a different level of study (e.g., from post-secondary to graduate education).
When applying to extend their study permit, the applicant will need to provide proof that they meet one of the exceptions, if they don't provide a PAL with their application.
If an applicant has applied for a study permit from within Canada IRCC will send a letter of approval in the applicant's online account to let them know their study permit has been approved. They can start studying as soon as they get that letter. Please note the applicant does not have to wait until they get their study permit in the mail to start studying

Question :
Can Somebody hold two work permits at the same time? If an applicant had an open work permit earlier with an expiry in 2026 and that same applicant got an lmia based work permit. Will the open work permit be valid? Can he/she work with other employers based on his previous open work permit?
Response :
An individual may hold both an open work permit and an employer-specific work permit at the same time, provided they comply with the conditions of each permit. IRCC Help Centre-Two Work Permits
Question: If an Applicant is in Canada on Post Graduation Work Permit and is offered an online Job in India. Can he/she do an online job for an Indian company? Can he/she claim points for foreign work experience after 1 year of that Job?
Response: Remote work for a foreign employer while residing, studying, or working in Canada may be eligible for Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points for foreign work experience under the skills transferability points, as outlined in Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system. It may also be considered eligible foreign work experience for the Federal Skilled Workers program, provided it meets the listed requirements.
Please note that the system does not currently capture remote work. When claiming remote work performed from Canada, please make sure to select the employer's country/territory. When an applicant is invited to apply, please submit an explanation detailing the remote work agreement and where the employer and employee are physically located. You may choose to submit additional employment records to support your work experience.
Question: Can an Applicant declare his/her spouse "non-accompanying" in the Express Entry Profile while that
spouse is staying with him/her in Canada on a temporary basis?
Response: Based on personal circumstances, the applicant has a choice to have their family members as accompanying or non-accompanying. Family members, including spouses, may be switched to accompanying or non-accompanying at any time before the application is finalized. However, when it comes to spouses, such change between ITA and the time the application for permanent residence is submitted may affect the CRS score, and may result in a refusal of the application, should the score drop below the invitation round cut-off.
Please note that all questions must be answered truthfully, and information must not be omitted or manipulated to gain additional CRS points. As per section 40(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, a permanent resident or a foreign national is inadmissible for misrepresentation for directly or indirectly misrepresenting or withholding material facts relating to a relevant matter that induces or could induce an error in the administration of this Act.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is conducted on a case-by-case basis, taking into consideration the specific circumstances and the supporting documentation available to the officer. It is the applicant's responsibility to provide sufficient documentation to demonstrate that they meet the requirements.
We trust that this information will be of assistance to you.
Thank you kindly,

Warm regards,
On Friday, 4 July 2025 at 14:24, wrote:
Thank you for your response. Please note that I was not seeking guidance on hypothetical scenarios but rather an interpretation of the IRPA and IRPR in the context of a specific hypothetical scenario.
1. I respectively disagree with your interpretation that the "[e]xpiry of their status" refers to the expiry of their current (or last) status document (WP, SP, VR), as this appears to conflict with IRPR, R183(5) and R181(1).
Extension of period authorized for stay
183 (5) Subject to subsection (5.1), if a temporary resident has applied for an extension of the period authonized for their stay and a decision is not made on the application by the end of the period authorized for their stay, theperiod is extended until
(a) the day on which a decision is made, if the application is refused; or
(b) the end of the new period authorized for their stay, if the application is allowed.
Applications for Extension of Authorization to Remain in Canada as a Temporary Resident Circumstances
181 (1) A foreign national may apply for an extension of their authorization to remain in Canada as a temporary resident if
(a) the application is made by the end of the period authorized for their stay; and
(b) they have complied with all conditions imposed on their entry into Canada.
An applicant on "maintained status", by definition having an expired status document, remains
authorized to stay ("in status") beyond the expiry of their original document, as per R183(5).
I contend that “[e]xpiry of their status' means the expiry date of the applicant's current status
document (work permit, study permit, visitor record)", applies only to the context of the initial
extension submission, which is the context in the referenced paragraph. The IRPR allows
authorized stay ("in status") beyond the expiry of the original status document when prescribed
conditions for extension are duly followed. Thus, in my hypothetical scenario 1-a, the applicant
should remain authorized to stay (in status) after the first refusal of the VR until a decision is made
on their work permit application.
3. I believe my question about whether the date of a decision is considered authorized stay was not addressed. The language in R183(5)(a) states the date of the decision, even in the case of a refusal, falls within the period of authorized stay, meaning the applicant remains in status on the decision day, and only becomes out of status the day after. However the updated OM appears to contradict IRPR.
Regards,

Response:
Please note that IRCC cannot provide guidance regarding specific case inquiries or hypothetical scenarios.
An applicant benefits from maintained status if they submit an application to extend or change the conditions of their stay before the expiry date on their status document
or, if no status document was issued, before the end of the 6-month period of
authorized stay for foreign nationals who entered Canada as a visitor.
If an applicant who previously held a work or study permit applies for a visitor record before the expiry of their permit, they may benefit from maintained status during the
processing period of the visitor record application, but they do not have the
authorization to work or study after the expiry of their permit.
An applicant only maintains their temporary resident status during the processing period of their application for extension if they submit the application before the expiry of their status and remain in Canada. “Expiry of their status” means the expiry date of the applicant's current status document (work permit, study permit, visitor record) or, for those who did not receive a status document, the end of the period of authorized stay for visitors (6 months from the date a foreign national entered Canada as a visitor).
An applicant does not have maintained status if they submit another application for extension after the expiry of their status document or the 6-month period mentioned above.

Please note that students changing programs of study in between post-secondary levels at the same DLl, can keep studying at their DLl with their current study permit as long as they still meet their study permit conditions. If they need to extend their study permit because they are starting a new program for example, they may need to submit a new provincial attestation letter (PAL) or territorial attestation letter (TAL). students changing DLls at the post-secondary level must apply for a new study permit and wait for approval before beginning studies at the new institution.
All temporary residents have an automatically imposed condition that they must leave Canada at the end of their authorized period of stay. However, as per section R181, a temporary resident may apply to extend their period of authorized stay before it ends. If they have done so, their period of authorized stay as a temporary resident is extended by law until a decision is made [R183(5)]. Such a person is considered to have legal status as a temporary resident during the processing period only as long as the person remains in Canada. As such, the student do not need to change their status to visitor.
As per R189, a study permit holder may continue their studies under the same conditions as their previous study permit until a decision is made on their extension application if they have applied to extend their stay in Canada as a student before the expiry of the permit and they remain in Canada. This is referred to as maintained status.
For further information on different scenarios based on level of study, please see Changing your school or program-Canada.ca.
For more information, please visit: Study Permits: Assessing study permit conditions-Canada.ca Temporary residents: Maintained status during processing (previously called implied status)

Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the RCC Web form.
Please see our response to your question.
The Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) is a de facto state recognized only by Turkey. Canada, along with most of the international community, considers this territory to be part of the Republic of Cyprus. As a result, TRNC does not appear as a selectable country on Canadian immigration forms. Therefore, applicants who have spent more than six consecutive months in TRNC should declare this time as time spent in the Republic of Cyprus, in line with Canada's official position. Police certificates (PCs) should be obtained accordingly.
To ensure transparency and avoid delays, applicants are encouraged to include a brief explanation in their application. This note can clarify that they were physically located in TRNC during that period. In some cases, it may be helpful to provide police certificates from both Turkey and Cyprus.
Regarding misrepresentation: this typically refers to knowingly providing false or incomplete information. If an applicant makes a genuine effort to be truthful and transparent, even if the format or method isn't perfect, it is unlikely to be considered misrepresentation.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is conducted on a case-by-case basis, taking into consideration the specific circumstances and the supporting documentation available to the officer. It is the applicant's responsibility to provide sufficient documentation to demonstrate that they meet the requirements.
We trust that this information will be of assistance to you.
Thank you kindly,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

In a scenario where an employer proposes to average an employee's overtime, with the employee's

Overtime is part of working conditions. As per 209,2(1)(a)(iii) and 209.3(1)(a)(iv) “...the employer must provide the foreign national with... wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer".
If an employer were providing working conditions that are substantially the same but not less favourable than what is outlined in the offer of employment, and if they were complying with the federal or provincial laws that regulate the employment or recruitment of employees, including foreign nationals, in the province in which the foreign national works, and if they were complying with all other subsections of R209.2 or R209.3, the arrangement would likely comply with the Regulations.

Merci d’avoir contacté la boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration.
Veuillez noter que cette boîte aux lettres est destinée à fournir des conseils généraux et ne fournit pas de réponses à des demandes spécifiques à un cas, mais a fourni les informations suivantes comme conseil. Veuillez consulter notre réponse à votre question.
Le service de transmission des demandes urgentes de permis de travail n'est ni une activité prescrite par la loi ni une décision fondée sur une délégation de pouvoir. Par conséquent, les demandes de traitement accéléré sont étudiées au cas par cas.
Les demandes de traitement d’urgence sont reçues le plus souvent lorsque les clients communiquent avece Centre de soutien à la clientèle pour demander un traitement urgent; lorsque des députés communiquent avec le centre de traitement des demandes pour demander un traitement d’urgence pour un de leurs électeurs; ou lorsque des bureaux locaux reçoivent des transmissions de demandes de traitement d’urgence directement de partenaires (par exemple, les gouvernements provinciaux).
La liste actuelle donne des exemples de cas qui justifient un traitement urgent : Un médecin étranger participant au traitement de patients (par exemple, un pathologiste qui traite des patients atteints du cancer) change d’employeur, déménage dans une autre province ou renouvelle son permis d’exercice de la médecine. (ll est à noter qu'un médecin enseignant qui ne participe pas activement au traitement de patients n’est pas admissible au traitement d’urgence.) Un travailleur étranger doit se déplacer de toute urgence pour un voyage d’affaires ou en raison d’un décès dans la famille ou d’une maladie grave. Un travailleur étranger est admissible au Programme de gestion des cas et de surveillance dans la collectivité (GCSC) faisant partie des solutions de rechange à la détention de l’Agence des services frontaliers du Canada (ASFC).
En cas de demande de traitement urgent, les clients doivent fournir une preuve de l’urgence de leur situation, comme une preuve de voyage, un certificat de décès, une preuve de maladie grave, ou une preuve d’inscription au Programme de GCSC.
Cordialement,
et Ciloyenneé Canada
