Si une demande d’engagement et DCSQ sont rejeté par le MIFI (immigration Quebec), est-ce que la demande de parrainage poursuit son cours ? ou sera-t-elle automatiquement refusée ?
Si la demande de parrainage n’est pas annulée, le répondant peut-il déposer de nouveau une DCSQ-engagement ou peut-il déménager de province et aviser IRCC du déménagement ?
Merci
Ghazal, Reda (IRCC/IRCC)
threads.answer:
1-Dec-25
Bonjour,
Merci d’avoir contacté la boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration.
Veuillez noter que cette boîte aux lettres est destinée à fournir des conseils généraux et ne fournit pas de réponses à des demandes spécifiques à un cas, mais a fourni les informations suivantes comme conseil. Si vous avez des questions spécifiques à un dossier, nous vous encourageons à soumettre le formulaire Formulaire Web d'IRCC-Canada.ca
Veuillez consulter notre réponse à votre question.
Lorsqu’une demande d’engagement et de Certificat de sélection du Québec (CSQ) est retournée par le Ministère de l’Immigration, de la Francisation et de l’Intégration (MiFl), en raison de l’atteinte du nombre maximal de demandes d’engagement pouvant être reçues actuellement, la demande de parrainage demeurera en traitement chez (IRCC). Le délai pour déposer la demande d’engagement et de CSQ sera prolongé et la demande de parrainage restera dans l’inventaire d’IRCC jusqu'à la reprise de la réception des demandes par le MIFI.
Selonle site Web du MIFl, le répondant pourra présenter une demande d'engagement lorsqu'une nouvelle période de réception des demandes sera ouverte. IRCC continuera de traiter la demande de parrainage une fois que le répondant aura déposé sa demande auprès du MIFl et obtenu une décision.
Dans le cas où le répondant était un résident du Québec au moment de la soumission de sa demande de parrainage à IRCC, mais qu'il a depuis déménagé dans une autre province ou un autre territoire pendant le traitement de la demande de parrainage et avant la délivrance d’un visa de résident permanent, IRCC devra procéder à sa propre évaluation financière du répondant. Lorsque le répondant aura déménagé hors du Québec, il devra en informer IRCC en envoyant un formulaire Web pour mettre à jour ses coordonnées.
Une fois satisfait que le répondant a déménagé à l’extérieur du Québec, IRCC effectuera sa propre évaluation de l’admissibilité au parrainage. Nous pourrions demander des formulaires de parrainage et des documents financiers à jour pour toutes les années d’imposition écoulées depuis la demande initiale, s’il y a lieu.
Nous espérons que vous trouverez ces informations utiles.
Cordialement,

I am writing to request clarification regarding the 2026 Home Child Care Provider Pilot and Home Support Worker Pilot. While reviewing the preliminary program information, I noticed
that some of the published requirements appear unclear and somewhat contradictory.
Specifically, the program indicates that applicants need only six (6) months of eligible work
experience or training, yet it also requires a full-time indeterminate job offer from a Canadian
employer. This has created confusion among applicants and representatives as to how both conditions are intended to work together.
A) Work Duration After Gaining Experience or Training:

and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
B) Previous Work Experience: If an applicant has already completed 6 months of eligible work experience in Canada within the last five years but was unable to apply under the previous pilot intake, can they still use that prior experience—supported by reference letters, pay stubs, and employment records—to apply for permanent residence under the upcoming 2026 program, even if they are now working in a different occupation? The delivery structure and operational instructions for the new program have not yet been made fully clear, and clarification would help ensure applications are submitted in full compliance with the intended program design. Your guidance on these matters would be greatly appreciated.
Best Regards

Ghazal, Reda (IRCC/IRCC)
threads.answer:
Support Worker and Child Care Provider Pilots (2026) - REP-B-2025-2127 - Due 2- Dec-25
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form.
Please see our response to your question.
To qualify under the Home Care Worker Immigration pilots, applicants must have enough relevant work experience OR training.
1. The work experience must have been gained within the 3 years before they apply.
1. Any experience gained after applying doesn't count.
2. be continuous, meaning they must have worked at least 6 months in a row
1. It may include a reasonable vacation period (for example, 2 weeks of paid leave within a 52-week period).
2. If they changed jobs, there must be no breaks between them.
3. be full-time, meaning at least 30 hours of paid work per week
1. If they worked multiple part-time jobs at the same time, it only counts if it adds up to at least 30 hours per week for 6 months in a row.
Applicants must also have a genuine job offer as home child care provider or home support worker. The job offer must be in the National Occupational Classification of the pilot they are applying for. Please see here for more information.
The job offer must be for full-time continuous work, meaning at least 30 hours of paid work per week and for permanent employment (no set end date). The officer processing the application may contact the employer at any point to request additional documentation to ensure the job offer is genuine.
As stated on the website: The job must be:
1. in the National Occupational Classification (NOC) of the pilot you apply for:
1. Home Care Worker Immigration Pilot: Child Care
1. Home child care providers (NOC 44100)
2. The location can't be an institutional setting such as a daycare.
3. A job as a foster parent doesn't count.
2. Home Care Worker Immigration Pilot: Home Support
1. Home support workers, caregivers and related occupations (NOC 44101)
2. The location can't be an institutional setting such as a nursing home.
We trust this information will assist you.
Thank you kindly,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Response 2:
The public policy is for applicants that meet the conditions, including (but limited to) submitting a work permit application or work permit renewal application under subsection 201(1) of the Regulations to perform work described in as per paragraphs 200(1)(c)(ii.1) or 200(1)(c)(iii) of the Regulations, and that intends to work for a new employer and/or occupation as specified by the job offer included in their work permit application, so that they may work for a new employer while waiting on a decision on their application.
The objectives of this public policy are to allow temporary foreign workers already in Canada who are changing jobs or employers, and who have secured a job offer under the terms of either the Temporary Foreign Worker Program or International Mobility Program, to more quickly begin work in advance of a final decision on the work permit application.
Noting that an applicant applying for a fully open work permit would not be covered by the public policy as they cannot fulfill the condition to intend to work for a new employer and/or occupation as specified by the job offer included in their work permit application. Response 2:
The public policy is for applicants that meet the conditions, including (but limited to) submitting a work permit application or work permit renewal application under subsection 201(1) of the Regúlations to perform work described in as per paragraphs 200(1)(c)(ii.1) or 200(1)(c)(iii) of the Regulations, and that intends to work for a new employer and/or occupation as specified by the job offer included in their work permit application, so that they may work for a new employer while waiting on a decision on their application.
The objectives of this public policy are to allow temporary foreign workers already in Canada who are changing jobs or employers, and who have secured a job offer under the terms of either the Temporary Foreign Worker Program or International Mobility Program, to more quickly begin work in advance of a final decision on the work permit application.
Noting that an applicant applying for a fully open work permit would not be covered by the public policy as they cannot fulfill the condition to intend to work for a new employer and/or occupation as specified by the job offer included in their work permit application. Only workers applying for an employer specific work permit can fulfill the requirement of having secured a job offer under the terms of either the Temporary Foreign Worker Program or International Mobility Program.
Q3: If the TFW applies for a BOWP and rely on the Policy, would they need to wait for any communication from IRCC before they are authorized to work in Canada under this Policy before a decision has been made?
Response 3:
See above response. Open work permit applicants are not covered by the public policy.

threads.subject: For review: FW: Policy clarification request – EMPP permanent residents and travel to country of nationality-REP-B-2025-2125 - Due 1-Dec-25
threads.question:
Dear IRCC colleagues,
I am an authorized representative requesting policy clarification regarding the Economic Mobility Pathways Pilot (EMPP).
As you know, individuals selected under the EMPP are processed through an economic immigration stream, rather than as protected persons under section 95 of the IRPA
My inquiry concerns individuals who have already landed in Canada and now hold permanent resident status obtained through the EMPP.
In traditional refugee protection cases, individuals are cautioned not to travel to their country of origin due to potential “re-
availment” concerns. Given that EMPP participants are economic immigrants, I seek clarification on whether similar
restrictions or policy considerations apply once they hold permanent resident status in Canada.
Specifically, could IRCC confirm whether temporary travel to their country of nationality has any implications for their Canadian permanent resident status or for a pending or future citizenship application, assuming the individual continues to meet all residence and admissibility requirements.
This request is for policy clarification only and does not relate to any specific client file. If possible, please direct me to any Program Delivery Instructions or operational guidance that address these matters.
Thank you for your time and assistance.
Kind regards,
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-
specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. If you have case specific
questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form. Please see our response to your question. *** The EMPP Public Policies do not restrict travel for EMPP Permanent Residents (PRs) after their arrival in Canada including to their country of origin. As such there may be no impact to their Permanent Resident status in Canada due to travelling to their country of origin after they arrive in Canada. However, it should be noted that travelling to their country of origin is not something that the department encourages due to the potential safety and/or security concerns for the client. Furthermore, it is important to be aware that as with any case, should information come to light that a client may
have misrepresented or withheld material facts in their permanent resident application, an investigation may be
launched which could result in enforcement action being taken including the loss of their permanent resident status.
Additionally, if clients are looking to travel internationally after their arrival in Canada, they will need to ensure that they have the required travel documents to do so. For example, if a client used a Single Journey Travel Documents issued by the department, to travel to Canada, they will not be able to use that document to travel from Canada after their arrival.
Clients may need to apply for Certificates of Identity after they arrive to enable international travel. It is important to note that some countries may not accept the Certificate of Identity as a valid travel document and clients should check with the consulate or embassy of the country that they wish to visit before travelling.
Thank you kindly,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Response: When minor children reach the age of majority (18 or 19 years old, depending on the province or territory), they must apply for a study permit if they want to keep studying, unless another exemption applies.

Response: Financial requirements apply to all applicants unless exempted under the regulations (e.g., scenarios described in R215(1)(d) or (e)). Applicants should provide documentation demonstrating their ability to support themselves during their studies, unless they fall under one of the exemptions.

Bonjour,
Récemment, la situation suivante est arrivée à 3 de nos clients :

- * Il soumet une demande pour prolonger son statut en ligne.
- * La lettre de confirmation d’envoi de la demande de prolongation de statut qui est normalement générée automatiquement dans la prochaine heure n’est toujours pas au dossier après plusieurs jours d’attente.
- * Selon l’état du dossier en ligne, nous voyons qu'un nouveau numéro lUC est attribué à ce client.
- * Le client a donc maintenant une demande de prolongation de statut lié à un mauvais numéro d’IUC.
- * Il a de la difficulté à démontrer à son employeur, à la RAMQ et à d’autres institutions qu’il va pouvoir conserver son statut après expiration de son permis actuel.
Nous avons envoyé un formulaire web pour signaler cette erreur et demander à l’IRCC de fusionner les deux dossiers, pour que le client puisse avoir sa demande traitée dans le bon dossier individuel et ainsi avoir les données biométriques au dossier et ne pas avoir à resoumettre d’autres sous un nouveau lUC.
En revanche, nous n’avons pas eu de retour pour les formulaires web envoyés à part un accusé de réception automatisé. Nous sommes inquiets que ces requêtes ne soient pas traitées avant 200+ jours (délais moyens de traitement de prolongation de permis de travail) et alors notre client sera dans une situation très précaire sans preuve de conservation de statut.
Merci de nous guider sur quoi faire dans ce genre de situation et comment nous pourrions accélérer ce processus pour avoir les lettres de confirmation d’envoi rapidement.
Cordialement,

We can confirm that this includes a situation where both spouses are physically present at the same location in the presence of witnesses, but with the celebrant attending online. The ceremony takes place where the celebrant is located. Therefore, if the two parties to the marriage are not in the same location as the celebrant, the parties to the marriage are not physically present at the marriage ceremony within the meaning of R117(9)(c.1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). As a result, this would be considered an online marriage, excluded for immigrations purposes.

Q4: What is IRCC's definition of enrolment for the purpose of this provision? Is it being active in the program or being enrolled in and taking classes? Students could be active in the program while on a scheduled break or an authorized leave, but they are not enrolled in classes during that time.
A4: A student is considered enrolled if they are actively attending classes or registered for courses at their DLI excluding regularly scheduled breaks, and authorized leave of up to 150 days. Students will need to ensure that they meet the conditions of their study permit Your conditions as a study permit holder in Canada-Canada.ca. Therefore, while students are not actively taking classes during regularly scheduled breaks or authorized leave of up to 150 days, they are still considered as being enrolled in their DLI.
Follow up questions:
- * If a student is registered in classes, but starts their program in let's say four months, are they considered enrolled at a DLI by IRCC for the purpose of this regulation for four months until they start classes? Every term, we have several students who are withdrawn from a program, but are planning to start a different program in one term.
- * If a student is withdrawn from a program, has a LOA for a different program that starts in 4 months, but is not registered in classes yet, are they considered enrolled at a DLI by IRCC for the purpose of this regulation for four months until they start classes?
Answer: As indicated above, a student is no longer registered or enrolled when the DLl has sent a letter informing the student that they've been dismissed, withdrawn or transferred to another institution. Their study permit becomes invalid as per R222(1)(a.1), even if the document is not expired. Please note that an academic withdrawal is not considered an authorized leave in which the student is no longer considered an active student. Therefore, they would need to change their status or leave Canada.
In comparison, an academic suspension would be considered a leave. A student may take leave for a maximum 150 days due to academic suspension and would not be considered as no longer being registered or enrolled. The student would be allowed to return to their studies after the suspension. Please note that the enrollment status as " no longer registered/enrolled" and " academic suspension" are not the same. Please note that any leave over 150 days is not allowed, and the student would either need to change their status or leave Canada.
The IRCC website provides a glossary with definitions about the enrollment status of a student at a DLl such as academic suspension, no longer registered or enrolled, authorized leave etc.

A1. For CRS purposes, education points are based on the level of completed education, as defined in the Ministerial Instructions.

Or, similar to Canadian credential requirements, must the program be at least 8 months in length, completed primarily in person, and pursued on a full-time basis?
A3. A foreign online program can qualify for the education points if the ECA confirms its equivalency to a Canadian credential.

I would like to seek clarification regarding the calculation of CRS scores and the definition of an accompanying versus non-accompanying spouse under the Express Entry system.
1. 1. In a scenario where only one spouse wishes to immigrate and live in Canada, can that spouse list the other as non-accompanying in their Express Entry profile and subsequent application? Is there any Ministerial Instruction, Program Delivery Instruction (PDI), or other IRCC policy guidance that defines or governs such cases?
2. 2. Additionally, if after the lock-in date (submission of the e-APR) the principal applicant's marital status changes — for example, the applicant gets married, or the previously non-accompanying spouse later decides to accompany — would this lead to a recalculation of CRS eligibility or reassessment of the ITA (after the e-APR)?
Answer:
1. 1. Yes, a principal applicant can list their spouse as non-accompanying in their Express Entry profile and e-APR, provided the spouse is truthfully declared and the designation is consistent with the applicant's intent. This is supported by (IRCC)'s Program Delivery Instructions on assessing Express Entry applications under section A11.2. Please note that it is an obligation for the applicant to declare all information truthfully and accurately. A spouse or a common-law partner must be declared on an application for permanent residence, whether the principal applicant intends for them to be accompanying or not. Failure to declare a spouse or a common-law partner or failure to provide accurate information regarding marital status on an application may result in misrepresentation
2. 2. No, changes to marital status or accompanying status after the lock-in date (submission of the e-APR) do not lead to a recalculation of the Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score or reassessment of the Invitation to Apply (ITA). According to IRCC's Program Delivery Instructions on assessing Express Entry applications under section A11.2, the applicant's eligibility and CRS score are assessed based on the information provided at the time of e- APR submission. This is considered the lock-in date, and any changes after that point—such as getting married or a non-accompanying spouse deciding to accompany—do not retroactively affect the CRS score or the ITA. Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form. Please see our response to your question. *** IRCC applies a weekly cap of 30 hours when calculating eligible work experience for Express Entry. Regardless of whether the work is full-time or part-time, any hours worked beyond 30 per week do not count toward the required 1,560 hours.
To calculate the hours for a period of work experience, the number of hours worked each week during that period is recorded, capped at 30 hours per week if exceeded, then added together, and then divided by the number of weeks in the period.
The work hours are calculated only when the applicant performs the duties under their occupation. Periods of leave or rest do not count as hours of performing the duties.
For fluctuating schedules — such as working 20 hours one week and 40 the next — hours are calculated based on actual time worked, but no more than 30 hours per week will be credited toward Express Entry eligibility.
In situations where regularly scheduled work throughout the year varies in hours from week to week, for example based on professional regulatory requirements, the hours of work may be averaged throughout the year and the officer would determine on a case-by-case basis if the hours declared could be reasonably considered as work experience. Please ensure there is a clear explanation in case hours declared in the profile do not exactly match hours worked.

threads.subject: Misrepresentation Finding - 5 year bar clarification? - REP-B-2025-2434 - Due 12-Jan-26
threads.question:
If a person was denied a visa to enter Canada based on a misrepresentation and thus given a 5 year bar from entering Canada per s. 40(2) of IRPA, and the Immigration Division (“ID”) also then found the person inadmissible for the very same misrepresentation and issued a five-year exclusion order (for example, a year or two later) –when can the person return to Canada, in view of this same findings having been made twice? Does IRCC agree that the 5-year bar ought to start to run from the first denial/determination outside of Canada, given that s. 40(2) does not clarify or contemplate findings made twice for the same reason, both inland and overseas on the same basis:
S. 40 (a) the permanent resident or the foreign national continues to be inadmissible for misrepresentation for a period of five years following, in the case of a determination outside Canada, a final determination of inadmissibility under subsection (1) or, in the case of a determination in Canada, the date the removal order is enforced; and
I was hoping to understand if there is an informal process or policy guidance, or simply an exercise of discretion, that may exist to address this through an internal recognition of the earlier start date. I understand new legislation is being proposed through Bill C-2 to clarify that the Immigration Division cannot take jurisdiction when a person is outside Canada, but that does not assist directly in answering this question and how this situation may be interpreted.
Thank you in advance for any assistance and information you can provide,
threads.answer:
Immigration Kepresentatives / Représentants immigration (IRCC)
Good day,
Thank you for your inquiry.
Based on an analysis of the A40 provision, IRCC interprets that the intent of A40(2)(a) was to invoke consequences for permanent residents or foreign nationals who are determined to be inadmissible for misrepresentation outside of Canada (via a final determination) or in Canada (via the enforcement of a removal order). While we believe that the intent was to address misrepresentation outside or inside of Canada, that does not limit the use of the provision, nor does it change the consequences if a permanent resident or foreign national were to become subject to both a final determination and an enforced removal order. That being said, IRCC interprets that if a person, as the result of misrepresentation, were to become subject of both a final determination outside of Canada and an enforced removal order, they would continue to be inadmissible for 5 years from the date that each occurred; or in the event they occurred within five years of each other, five years from the date of the most recent.
Using your scenario, if a person was denied a visa based on misrepresentation (and became subject to a final determination), and subsequently (a year or two later), became subject to an enforced removal order, then they would be inadmissible for five years from the date the removal order was enforced.
It is unclear whether or not your scenario is hypothetical, as if such a situation were to occur there would be a few things to be explained:
- * if the person was denied a visa to Canada based on misrep, then it's reasonable to assume that they were outside of Canada at the time of refusal. Otherwise, a refusal of their visa based on misrep would not invoke the five year final determination inadmissibility.
- * Providing that the person was outside of Canada at the time of refusal and final determination, and therefore is subject to the five year inadmissibility, it is unclear how the individual would gain access to Canada. As you're aware, the individual would need to be in Canada to become the subject of a removal order, which is enforced when they leave. If the person did gain access to Canada despite being inadmissible as a result of the final determination, then they would only have been able to do so by either misrepresenting on a visa application again, or by entering Canada without authorization, both of which would form the basis of a “new” inadmissibility.
- * All that being said, it seems rather unlikely that the scenario you've provided would occur in reality.
Finally, for clarity: a final determination outside of Canada that a person is inadmissible for misrepresentation, or the enforcement of a removal order that was issued on the same grounds, does not result in a “bar from entering Canada”. Rather, it renders the individual inadmissible for misrepresentation for five years from the date of the determination / enforcement. As with other inadmissibilities, relief is available, for example a TRP, H&C etc, subject to the officer's discretion.
We hope this is of assistance.
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox
Citoyenneté Canada

threads.subject: Clarification on the authorized use of co-op work permits-REP-B-2025-2079 - Due 25-Nov-25
threads.question:
I am writing to request clarification on the authorized use of co-op work permits for international students enrolled in academic programs with mandatory work-integrated learning components.
Specifically, we are seeking guidance on the following scenario:
A program includes a mandatory co-op component requiring a minimum of 400 hours to be completed within a 15-week period. The program does not specify a maximum number of hours that a student may work during this period.
Would IRCC consider it authorized for students to continue working under their co-op work permit beyond the 400-hour
minimum, provided they do not exceed the 15-week duration defined by the program?
In other words, is any work performed under the co-op work permit beyond the minimum hourly requirement, but still within the approved program timeframe, considered compliant with IRCC regulations?
We appreciate your guidance on this matter to ensure institutional practices remain aligned with federal immigration policy and to support international students in maintaining valid status while fulfilling academic requirements.
threads.answer:
Exemption code C32 (co-op for post-secondary international students) is intended for foreign nationals who intend to perform work that is an essential part of a post-secondary academic, vocational or professional training program offered by a designated learning institution (DLI) in Canada. The work cannot form more than 50% of the total program of study.
The acceptance letter provided by the DLl should clearly establish that the work is an essential part of the academic, vocational or professional training program that all participants enrolled in the program are required to complete in order to receive their degree, diploma or certificate.
The determination of what work is considered an essential part of the program is made by the DLI.
Work related to a research, educational or training program-Exemption codes C31, C32 and C33 (International Mobility Program [IMP]) - Canada.ca
Thank you,

Ukraine ends temporary passport

Sunday, 2 November 2025, 14:01 Foreign passport. UNIAN As reported by Department of the Consular Service of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine As of October 29, 2025, the Cabinet of Ministers has canceled the temporary extension of the validity of foreign passports and the requirement to include information about children in the documents. This measure was introduced at the outset of the full-scale invasion as an exceptional procedure. The Department of Consular Service of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine explained that the temporary order came into force in February 2022 when Ukraine's passport system failed and could not issue new documents. The system is now fully restored. New biometric passports can be issued both abroad at embassies and consulates, and at branches of the State Enterprise “Document" abroad. The MFA emphasizes that Ukraine is returning to international standards, as most countries do not recognize passports with extended validity or a document without a separate proof of identity for a child. Such changes create conveniences and reduce problems at border crossings.
Key changes and standards
Citizens whose passport validity is expiring must obtain a new biometric document. The validity of a passport for persons aged 16 and over is a maximum of 10 years. The validity of a passport for children under 16 is a maximum of 4 years. Having a separate international passport is mandatory for every citizen, including children.
mmigration, Réfugiés and Cizenship Canedaot Cioyenneté Canada
Recommendations for citizens
When attempting to travel from Ukraine to the EU with a passport that has extended validity or with a child listed in the passport, border guards of the EU country are most likely not to permit entry. In such a case, it is advisable to obtain a new passport in Ukraine. If, upon returning to Ukraine from the EU (or another country), border guards do not allow crossing with such a document, you should contact the nearest Ukrainian embassy or consulate. They will issue an “identity document for return to Ukraine" (the so-called “white passport’). The document is issued on the day of application; for children under 16 years of age it is free.
Air travel and restrictions
Regarding air travel: in line with ICAO standards, carriers have the right to refuse boarding to a passenger with an extended passport. The MFA also reminded that Ukrainian law allows every citizen to have two valid foreign passports.
In summary, the new rules bring Ukrainians back to global standards of document issuance. Plan to renew documents in advance, check validity dates, and consider the possibility of owning two valid international passports if you travel frequently.

Good day,
Thank you for your inquiry. Please note that the information provided serves as general program guidance and should not be considered a directive for case-specific inquiries.
Questions: Yorkville University maintains partnership agreements (MOUs) with several institutions in Canada and internationally. We would appreciate your guidance on the PAL requirements for the following scenarios:
- * English Pathway Program with ILSC o* Yorkville University has a partnership with ILSC to offer an English pathway program that serves as a route into our bachelor's degree programs. In this scenario, would it be acceptable for students to submit only a PAL issued by Yorkville University when applying for their study permit? Additionally, would this arrangement be considered a joint program under current IRCC guidelines?
- * Partnership with St. Claire College o* Under this agreement, students complete a diploma in Interior Design at St. Claire College and subsequently transfer to Yorkville University to complete the Bachelor of Interior Design. Students receive separate credentials from each institution (Diploma from St. Claire and a bachelor's degree from Yorkville University). In this case, would this arrangement be considered a joint program? Furthermore, would it be acceptable for students to submit only a PAL from Yorkville University and study at both institutions under a single study permit?
Response Ajoint program is defined as one that results in a single credential issued by one designated learning institution (DLl), even if multiple DLls deliver parts of the program. Students require:
- * One provincial/territorial attestation letter (PAL/TAL) from the province or territory of the credential-issuing DLI.
- * One study permit naming the credential-issuing DLl for the entire duration of their studies (or until passport expiry, whichever comes first).
If students receive two distinct credentials (e.g., a diploma from one institution and a degree from another), this is not considered a joint program. In these cases:
- * Students may require a PAL/TAL for each institution.
- * A new study permit may be required when transitioning between DLls.
Language or other preparatory programs offered by a separate DLl are not considered part of a joint program unless they are integrated into a single credential. Students generally need a PAL/TAL for the institution where they will study first and may need to apply for a new study permit for subsequent programs.
Please visit IRCC websites for more details: Changing your school or program-Canada.ca Study permit: Get the right documents Provincial attestation letter or territorial attestation letter-Canada.ca

threads.question:
Good day,
Question:
IRCC guidance confirms that maintained status ends when a temporary resident departs Canada during the processing of a visitor record extension. What remains unclear is what happens if IRCC approves that visitor record extension after the person has already left and then re-entered Canada:
- * Does IRCC consider the approval of the visitor record extension to be nullified once the applicant departs, meaning their stay after re-entry is governed solely by the period granted by CBSA at the port of entry (typically six months)? OR
- * Should CBSA officers honour the approved visitor record issued by IRCC after the person's re-entry?
Which governs the client's lawful period of stay after re-entry: the approved extension or the new entry authorization?
Thank you for your guidance!
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
This information is provided as general policy guidance and is not a directive for individual case files. For case- specific enquiries, applicants can contact the Department by submitting the IRCC Web form.
A visitor record indicates that the holder has temporary resident status in Canada and how long they can stay. lt doesn't guarantee that they can leave and then re-enter Canada. If a temporary resident leaves Canada while their visitor record application is in process, then it is no longer possible to extend their authorized period of stay, as it ended when they left Canada, as per R183(4). On entry, if the officer does not fix a period of authorized stay (by means of a stamp or a VR), then the foreign national is authorized to stay for 6 months from the date of entry, or until the expiry of their passport or biometrics (whichever comes first), as per R183(2).

Response 1 IRCĆ classifies educational programs into three main levels:
1. 1. Primary and secondary education
2. 2. Post-secondary education (including vocational/technical training and undergraduate programs)
3. 3. Graduate education or above (master's and PhD)
Applicants do not require a new study permit when changing programs within the same level at the same designated learning institution (DLl). However, a new study permit is required when changing DLls at the post-secondary level or moving between levels.

Question 3 Are graduate certificates or diplomas considered "post-secondary level" or "graduate studies or above"?
Response 3 Graduate-level programs remain classified as graduate studies, regardless of whether the credential is a degree or a certificate/diploma. IRCC does not differentiate based on credential type alone; the determining factor is the level of study (graduate vs. undergraduate).

L'nmdudion these conditions, they may require the student to leave Canada. This could impact the outcome of any future applications, and the student may need to wait six months before reapplying for a study permit, visitor visa, or work permit. Additionally, if a student is unenrolled (withdrawn) by the Designated Learning Institution (DLl) due to unauthorized leave or other academic reasons, their study permit will become invalid. Question 2: If a student applies to return to their studies after being out of school on an unscheduled break for one semester,
does that student need to restore their status prior to returning to their approved DLi?
Answer: No, restoration of status applies when the study permit has expired, and the student had met study permit conditions. An unauthorized leave is considered a breach of study permit conditions. Even though, a student may have taken an unscheduled break/unauthorized leave for less than 150 days, there can be consequences on future applicants as indicated above. Therefore, it is important to ensure that students take authorized leave only. Students who are overseas and who have not met their previous study permit conditions, should apply for a new study permit with all the proper documentations. Please note that foreign nationals re-entering Canada as study permit holders will be assessed by a border service officer and should have all the necessary documentations in their
possessions regarding their studies if asked.

If a dependent family member arrives at a Canadian port of entry holding a valid PR visa before the principal applicant's PR status is fully finalized (i.e., the principal applicant is in Canada and eligible for virtual landing, but the eCOPR has not yet been issued).
And the CBSA/IRCC officer admits the dependent as a visitor instead of completing their PR landing, therefore the Confirmation of Permanent Residence (COPR) for the dependent remains unsigned.
1. 1. What is the landing procedure for this dependent, given that the one-time PR visa has already been used, and they were admitted only as a visitor? Response: A Border Service Officer (BSO) will not generally authorize the entry of a foreign national (FN) as a temporary resident (TR) when they hold a permanent resident visa (PRV). However, in cases where the FN is not seeking entry to become a permanent resident (PR), the BSO may authorize the FN into Canada as a TR if they hold the required TR documents, are satisfied they are admissible, and will leave at the end of their authorized stay. Generally, when a dependant (DEP) seeks entry to Canada before the principal applicant (PA) is processed for PR (who is in Canada), the B$O will facilitate the FN by authorizing entry under section 23 (entry for further examination) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). Once the PA is virtually landed, the DEP(s) return to the port of entry (POE) to have their examination completed (i.e. to be landed). Please note:
* If the BSO authorizes entry under section 23 of IRPA for the purpose of further examination, this does not give the DEP(s) TR status.
- * BSOs use the examination process on a case-by-case assessment how they will deal with a DEP who seeks entry prior to the PA becoming a PR. There is no guarantee they will be authorized entry under section 23.
* In the passport request letter, clients are instructed not to travel to Canada prior to the PA becoming a PR.
mmigration, Refugees
2. 2. Can such a dependent request virtual landing in Canada? If yes, what is the procedure? Response: Clients can be virtually landed if they have TR status in Canada; otherwise, they must be landed at a POE. If the DEP(s) were admitted as TRs, they must inform IRCC via Web form. They will then be provided with instructions explaining the next steps needed to confirm their PR status online through the PR Portal.
3. 3. Can the dependent attempt to re-enter Canada using the same PR visa again? Response: If a FN is authorized entry as a TR, the PRV will not be used (crossed out). It can therefore be presented on any subsequent entry where the foreign national seeks entry to become a PR, as long as it remains valid.

threads.answer:
Good day, Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form. Please see our response to your question. *** Given the complex situation on the ground faced by clients with documents from Crimea, IRCC handles these cases on a case-by-case basis, leveraging various mechanisms in the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) such as temporary resident permits (A24), humanitarian and compassionate considerations (A25), and Single Journey Travel Documents when a delegated decision maker determines that is appropriate.
Marriage, as defined in subsection 1(1) of the IRPR, is defined in respect of a marriage that took place outside Canada, as “a marriage that is valid both under the laws of the jurisdiction where it took place and under Canadian law”.
Documents issued by Russia in Crimea and other parts of occupied Ukraine are not considered legally valid under Ukrainian laws. As Canada considers Crimea to be occupied Ukrainian territory, IRCC respects this Ukrainian legal position and does not recognize marriage certificates issued by Russian authorities.
Based on best available information, it is our current understanding that Ukraine can recognize an act of marriage through court decision, which provides a potential route for legal recognition of a marriage that has already occurred in occupied territory. Russian-issued Crimean marriage certificates may be used along with witness testimonies, photos, and other evidence to support an application to a Ukrainian court. If the court is satisfied that a marriage took place and is in accord with Ukrainian laws, then a court decision will be issued. This formal court decision can then be used to register the marriage officially with the Ukrainian State Register of Civil Status Acts (DRATS) and to obtain a legally valid Ukrainian marriage certificate.
Importantly, certification of Crimean marriage documents by Russian authorities would not be acceptable as it does not resolve the problem of the marriage and its registration being non-compliant with Ukrainian laws. IRCC may recognize a *new* marriage if it took place and was registered in Mainland Russia or elsewhere; however, it is possible that this may cause administrative complications. Russian or other foreign authorities may not allow the registration of a second marriage, or they may require a divorce in Crimea before allowing a new marriage to be performed and registered elsewhere.
For this particular case where the couple has been married since 2023, they could be treated as common-law partners if an officer is satisfied that they meet the legal definition of common law partner (e.g. an individual who is cohabiting with the person in a conjugal relationship, having so cohabited for a period of at least one year – must provide evidence of cohabitation). The officer must also be satisfied that the relationship is not in bad faith.
If they have not yet cohabited for at least a year, they would not meet the legal definition of a common-law partner in R1(1). While conjugal partners do exist in R2, this provision has been used to allow for Family Class sponsorship of those unable to legally marry or cohabit as they are defined as “in relation to a sponsor, a foreign national residing outside Canada who is in a conjugal relationship with the sponsor and has been in that relationship for a period of at

Linformation divulguée en vertu de la loi sur l’accés à Finformation least one year". Accordingly, our understanding is that because Economic PR applications (such as Provincial Nominees) do not involve sponsorship, Crimean newlyweds without cohabitation would not meet the standard legal definition of a family member. ***

If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form Please see our response to your question. *** According to recent ministerial instructions, IRCC categorizes levels of study into three groups:
1. 1. Primary and secondary education

3. 3. Graduate education or above
Certificates, diplomas, and advanced diplomas (e.g., bachelor's degrees) all fall under post-secondary education. Students changing programs within the same level at the same Designated Learning Institution (DLl) do not need a new Provincial Attestation Letter (PAL) or territorial attestation letter (TAL). They can continue their studies at their DLl with their current study permit, provided they meet the permit conditions. However, if they need to extend their study permit, they must submit à new PAL/TAL.

If the Master program is considered as a graduate program at your DLI then students transitioning from a post secondary education level to a graduate level of education, must apply for a new study permit.
Students who remain within the same level of study while changing programs at the same designated learning institution (DLl) do not require a new PAL/TAL when applying for a study permit extension. For example, if the student wishes to change from one post-secondary program to another post-secondary program at the same DLI. However, a new PAL/TAL would be required if the student moves to a different level of study (e.g., from post-secondary to graduate education).
When applying to extend their study permit, the applicant will need to provide proof that they meet one of the exceptions if they don't provide a PAL with their application.
If an applicant has applied for a study permit from within Canada IRCC will send a letter of approval in the applicant's online account to let them know their study permit has been approved. threads.subject: Clarification regarding study permit & starting of study (Inside Canada) - REP-B-2025-2537 - Due 27-Jan-26
threads.question:
Dear IRCC Representative Mailbox Team,
I am seeking a general clarification regarding starting of studies after study permit approval inside Canada.
If a study permit application is approved from inside Canada, is the applicant allowed to start their studies immediately, or do they need to
wait until the actual study permit is delivered?
Waiting for your kind clarification regarding this.
Thanks,
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form. Please see our response to your question. *** If a student applies for a study permit from within Canada using the form IMM 5709, and the application is approved, they will receive:
- * An approval letter in their online account confirming that the study permit has been approved.
- * The physical study permit, which will be mailed to the Canadian address provided.
Students may begin their studies as soon as they receive the approval letter in their online account. They do not need to wait for the physical study permit to arrive by mail before staring their program.
For more details, please visit IRCC webpages: Study permit: After you apply-Canada.ca
We trust that this information will assist you.
Thank you kindly,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox
